title: power_mean_monotone: Unified Three-Case Proof
content: The main theorem proves M_r ≤ M_s for all r ≤ s with r, s ≠ 0. The proof uses rcases on the sign of r and s: when r > 0 (and hence s > 0), it delegates to power_mean_monotone_pos from AmgmInequalityOQ03; when r < 0 and s < 0, it delegates to power_mean_monotone_neg; when r < 0 < s, it delegates to power_mean_monotone_crossing_zero from PowerMeanCrossZeroOQ. These three cases are exhaustive since both r and s are nonzero. The unification collapses three gallery proofs into a single four-line case split.
mathContext: $M_r(x,w) \le M_s(x,w)$ for $r \le s$, $r,s \ne 0$, $w_i > 0$, $\sum w_i = 1$, $x_i > 0$. Case analysis: $(0 < r \le s)$ via Jensen for convex $t^{s/r}$; $(r \le s < 0)$ via Jensen for concave $t^{s/r}$ then reciprocal flip; $(r < 0 < s)$ via $M_r \le \text{GM} \le M_s$.

title: Case Split Strategy: Exhaustive Sign Analysis on r and s
content: The proof performs rcases (linear trichotomy) on the sign of r first, then on the sign of s. Since r ≤ s and both are nonzero, the cases are: (1) r > 0 ⟹ s > 0 (positive case), (2) r < 0 and s < 0 (negative case), (3) r < 0 and s > 0 (crossing zero — the novel case). The case r > 0 and s < 0 is impossible given r ≤ s. This exhaustive structure is the key insight: instead of a single uniform proof, the three partial results from the gallery interlock perfectly at the sign boundaries.
mathContext: Case tree: `rcases lt_or_eq_of_le hr : r ≠ 0` splits into $r > 0$ and $r < 0$. For $r > 0$: $s \ge r > 0$, apply pos case. For $r < 0$: `rcases hs` splits into $s < 0$ (neg case) and $s > 0$ (crossing-zero case). The case $r > 0 > s$ is excluded by $r \le s$.
prerequisites: the three partial power mean theorems

title: The Crossing-Zero Case: GM as Bridge
content: The most novel case is r < 0 < s, where the power mean exponent crosses zero. This cannot be handled by Jensen's inequality directly (the convexity of t^{s/r} breaks down when s/r < 0). Instead, the geometric mean M_0 = GM serves as a bridge: M_r ≤ GM ≤ M_s. The left inequality (M_r ≤ GM for r < 0) is proved in PowerMeanCrossZeroOQ via AM-GM applied to reciprocals; the right inequality (GM ≤ M_s for s > 0) is the classical weighted AM-GM. This factoring through GM is why the gallery needed a separate proof file for the crossing-zero case.
mathContext: $r < 0 < s$: $M_r \le \text{GM} \le M_s$ where $\text{GM}(x,w) = \prod x_i^{w_i} = \lim_{r\to 0} M_r$. Left: $M_r \le \text{GM}$ via AM-GM for $t^{-1}$ convex. Right: $\text{GM} \le M_s$ via weighted AM-GM ($\ln$ concavity). The bridge $M_0 = \text{GM}$ is the $r=0$ limiting value.

title: Corollaries: Classical Mean Inequalities as One-Liners
content: With power_mean_monotone proved, all classical pairwise mean comparisons become one-line applications: hm_le_am (r=-1, s=1), hm_le_qm (r=-1, s=2), am_le_qm (r=1, s=2). The power_mean_chain theorem proves transitivity M_r ≤ M_u ≤ M_s by two applications of the main theorem. This demonstrates the compactness of the unified approach: nine theorems in the corollary section are all direct applications, requiring no new mathematical ideas.
mathContext: HM $\le$ AM: $\frac{n}{\sum x_i^{-1}} \le \frac{\sum x_i}{n}$ (apply theorem at $r=-1, s=1$). AM $\le$ QM: $\frac{\sum x_i}{n} \le \sqrt{\frac{\sum x_i^2}{n}}$ (apply at $r=1, s=2$). Transitivity: $r \le u \le s \Rightarrow M_r \le M_u \le M_s$ by `power_mean_monotone` twice then `le_trans`.

title: HM ≤ GM ≤ AM ≤ QM: The Complete Mean Chain
content: The capstone theorem hm_le_gm_le_am_le_qm assembles the full classical chain. Three steps: HM ≤ GM (M_{-1} ≤ M_0, from PowerMeanCrossZeroOQ's power_mean_le_geom_mean_neg), GM ≤ AM (M_0 ≤ M_1, from geom_mean_le_power_mean_pos — the classical weighted AM-GM inequality), and AM ≤ QM (M_1 ≤ M_2, from the unified theorem). The use of two results from PowerMeanCrossZeroOQ for the GM-adjacent steps reflects that the geometric mean r=0 is the boundary case not covered by the unified theorem (which requires r,s ≠ 0).
mathContext: $M_{-1} \le M_0 \le M_1 \le M_2$: HM $\le$ GM $\le$ AM $\le$ QM. In closed form: $\frac{n}{\sum x_i^{-1}} \le \prod x_i^{1/n} \le \frac{\sum x_i}{n} \le \sqrt{\frac{\sum x_i^2}{n}}$ (uniform weights). Equality holds throughout iff all $x_i$ are equal.
